newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks, brokers told to beef up morals.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks, brokers told to beef up morals.

text.p: Japan's financial institutions were served with a strong warning on Friday to respect the law and beef up corporate ethics or face stiffer penalties in the forthcoming era of deregulated markets.

The architects of a "Big Bang" blueprint for Japanese market liberalisation that was unveiled on Friday called on firms to pursue aggressive reforms to restore confidence in the sector after a series of scandals.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also instructed ministers to work on strengthening the penalties for financial crime to ensure companies which flout the law pay a heavy price.

"Those scandals are regrettable at a time when Japan is implementing financial system reforms and financial institutions must try to regain confidence by complying with laws and beefing up corporate morals," a set of advisory panels to the finance minister said in a joint statement after unveiling their reform recommendations.
"We would like to strongly request that financial institutions reform themselves to make themselves suited for the financial system in the 21st century," they said.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters on Friday that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had instructed him and the justice minister to strengthen Japan's banking law to punish wrongdoers more harshly. Recent scandals have stirred criticism that punishments for white-collar crime are too mild.
However, the panels which unveiled their proposals on Friday did not go into detail on heavier penalties.
The chairman of the Financial System Research Council, one of the advisory bodies, told reporters stricter penalties were needed to act as a deterrent and prevent financial scandals.

"What I really feel sorry about is that there is a scandal which is beyond my comprehension. On that point, (regulators) should deal strictly with any violation of the rules," said Ryuichiro Tachi, the council's chairman.

A racketeer payoff scandal involving Japan's top brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd and leading commercial bank Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) has fanned worries about lax corporate governance and disclosure in a deregulated environment.

On Friday, further DKB executives including vice president Ichiro Fujita were arrested by prosecutors on suspicion of involvement in a scandal over suspected payoffs to a corporate extortionist, or "sokaiya".
The scandal, which came to light in March, has led to a host of arrests including 10 DKB officials, a former Nomura president and two racketeers at the heart of the affair.
Earlier on Friday, three advisory panels announced final proposals that Hashimoto had requested as blueprint for realising his "Big Bang" plans for deregulated financial markets by 2001.
The Financial System Research Council said that Japanese banks have fallen behind their overseas rivals, hobbled by bad debts left by the collapse of the late 1980s bubble economy.
While dealing with drastic financial reforms, banks must improve their asset quality as soon as possible, it said.

The council also urged the government to consider strengthening penalties for financial firms which submit false reports to authorities and called on the government to draw up steps to protect investors and boost the public's awareness of the need to take responsibility for their investments.

Separately, another panel, the Securities and Exchange Council, urged regulators to impose harsher penalties for illegal stock transactions, such as insider trading and stock manipulation, in line with global standards.

The government is expected to submit bills to parliament this autumn to tighten penalties for such wrongdoing and to allow financial institutions to establish holding companies, Finance Ministry officials said.
